title: ROLAND: Graph Learning Framework for Dynamic Graphs

problem.claim: Dynamic graph learning must address limitations in model design, evaluation settings, and training strategies.

gap.claim: Existing dynamic GNNs omit state-of-the-art static-GNN designs, use evaluation settings that do not fully reflect graph evolution, and rely on training methods that are not scalable.

contributions.claim: ROLAND is a graph representation learning framework that enables researchers to repurpose static GNNs for dynamic graphs.
The framework represents node embeddings at different GNN layers as hierarchical node states and recurrently updates them over time.
ROLAND introduces a live-update evaluation setting and a scalable training approach based on incremental training and meta-learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across eight dynamic graph datasets on future link prediction, ROLAND models achieved an average 62.7% relative MRR improvement over state-of-the-art baselines under standard evaluation settings on three datasets.
The authors report that state-of-the-art baselines encountered out-of-memory errors on larger datasets, whereas ROLAND scaled to dynamic graphs with 56 million edges.
After the baselines were re-implemented with the ROLAND training strategy, ROLAND models retained an average 15.5% relative MRR improvement.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs have been successful on static graphs, but that success has not fully transferred to dynamic graphs.
Dynamic GNNs face limitations in model design, evaluation realism, and training scalability.
ROLAND repurposes static GNNs through hierarchical recurrent node-state updates, adds live-update evaluation, and uses incremental training with meta-learning.
Experiments on eight dynamic graph datasets evaluate future link prediction and report improvements over baselines.
The authors report scalability to graphs with 56 million edges while baselines encounter out-of-memory errors.

source_observation.claim: Static GNN designs may be reusable for dynamic graphs when node representations are treated as evolving hierarchical states.

interpretation.claim: Separating static message-passing design from temporal state updating can simplify adaptation to dynamic settings.

application.claim: When adapting a static graph model to streaming data, consider recurrent updates over layer-wise representations.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this adaptation works for graph tasks beyond the reported future link prediction experiments.

source_observation.claim: Live-update evaluation is intended to mimic prediction and model updates on a rolling basis.

interpretation.claim: Evaluation protocols can materially affect how well dynamic graph methods reflect real-world use.

application.claim: Dynamic graph systems should be evaluated under protocols that preserve temporal evolution and rolling updates.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the exact live-update protocol or its comparison against the standard setting.

unknowns: The identities and characteristics of the eight datasets are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide model architectures, hyperparameters, training costs, or implementation details.
The exact baseline implementations, evaluation splits, and statistical variability are unspecified.
The scope of the reported improvements across datasets and tasks is not fully detailed.
